chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Ismail ibn Bazie, from Muhammad ibn al-Fudayl, from Abu al-Subah al-Kinani, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

There were young boys in the time of Ali (peace be upon him) who were playing with their toys, so one of them threw his toy at the other and broke his four front teeth. This matter was raised to the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him), so the thrower established the evidence that he had said, 'Beware, beware!' So he (peace be upon him) staved off the retaliation (qisas) from him, then said: 'He has excused himself, the one who cautioned.'

He (the narrator) said: 'And I asked him (peace be upon him) about a man killed by retaliation (qisas), is there wergild (diyah) for him?' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'If it were so, no one would be retaliated from; and the one who is killed by the legal penalty (hadd), there is no wergild for him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on wergild for accidental injury and execution in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* illustrates the application of *dar'* (exemption from retaliation) in cases of accidental injury, where the thrower's verbal warning ('Beware') served as sufficient proof of due care. Imam Ali (peace be upon him) used this to establish that liability is removed when the actor has taken reasonable precautions, a principle foundational to Shia jurisprudence on *daman* (compensation). The narration further clarifies that those executed for a fixed legal punishment (*hadd*) are not entitled to *diyah* (blood money), distinguishing between judicial execution and accidental death.
